title: Open Problems
intro: The questions quantum reservoir computing has not answered yet, from echo state conditions to measurement-efficient learning and a demonstrated advantage, with a self-test across the shelf.

items: Sharp echo state conditions. Sufficient conditions exist (strict contractivity of every $\mathcal{T}_s$ in some norm; see Martínez-Peña and Ortega), but practical reservoirs are often not strictly contractive in any one step and forget only over several. A computable, tight criterion for a given Hamiltonian, encoding and noise model is open.

Capacity with shots. Information-processing capacity is well defined for exact features. How it scales with $n$ at fixed shot budget $S$, and which dynamics maximise $N_{\text{eff}}(S)$, is largely unknown beyond numerics.

The role of the dynamical regime. Numerics show performance peaking near the transition between localized and ergodic regimes (Martínez-Peña and co-authors). Whether that is a general principle (an edge-of-chaos analogue for quantum systems) or specific to the models studied is open.

Encoding theory. The function class is fixed by how $\mathcal{T}_s$ depends on $s$. A systematic theory of encodings for time series, comparable to the Fourier-spectrum picture for parameterised circuits, would tell designers which encoding a task needs.

Avoiding concentration with expressivity. Concentration rules out generic scrambling, while simulability rules out the easiest structured dynamics. Which reservoirs sit between the two, hard to simulate and still with input-sensitive local features, is the central theoretical question for any advantage.

Online learning without restarts. Weak measurements, partial readout and rewinding each trade memory, signal and back-action differently (Mujal and co-authors; Yasuda and co-authors). An optimal protocol for a given task and device is not known.

Measurement as a resource. Mid-circuit measurements with feed-forward add nonlinearity and dissipation; how to design them as part of the reservoir rather than as a cost is just starting to be explored.
Choosing observables. Random Pauli sets, classical shadows and correlators all trade shot cost against feature diversity; which set to read for a given shot budget is an open optimisation problem.

Scaling studies. Most experiments show one system size. Accuracy and cost as functions of $n$, on the same platform and task, at realistic shot counts, would show whether there is a trend worth chasing.

Tasks with a reason to be quantum. Quantum-data tasks (classifying states, estimating entanglement, processing sensor outputs without tomography) and physically generated time series are the most plausible places for an advantage; benchmarks like NARMA are useful for debugging but solvable by small polynomial models.
Standard benchmarks and baselines. The field lacks an agreed suite with fixed data, splits, shot budgets and classical baselines; results are hard to compare across papers.

Noise as part of the design. Results suggest that some noise helps (Kubota and co-authors; Sannia and co-authors). Engineering device noise to set the memory time, instead of minimising it, is an open hardware question.

blocks.title: Echo state property in one line
blocks.text: State the echo state property for a quantum reservoir $\rho_k = \mathcal{T}_{s_k}(\rho_{k-1})$, and the simplest sufficient condition for it.
solution: Property: for any two initial states $\rho_0, \rho_0'$ and any input sequence, $\Vert\rho_k - \rho_k'\Vert_1 \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$; the state becomes a function of the input history alone.

Sufficient condition: every $\mathcal{T}_s$ is strictly contractive in trace norm on traceless operators, $\Vert\mathcal{T}_s(X)\Vert_1 \le \lambda\Vert X\Vert_1$ with $\lambda < 1$ uniform in $s$; then the distance shrinks at least as $\lambda^k$.
blocks.answer: Initial-state dependence vanishes; uniform strict contractivity suffices

blocks.title: Why only the readout is trained
blocks.text: Give two reasons, one computational and one physical, that reservoir computing trains only the linear readout.
solution: Computational: the training problem is ridge regression, convex with a closed-form solution, so there are no barren plateaus and no gradient estimation on hardware.

Physical: the reservoir is natural, fixed dynamics (an analog device, a noisy processor) whose parameters may not even be precisely known or controllable; reservoir computing only needs it to be repeatable.
blocks.answer: Convex closed-form training; uncontrolled physical dynamics suffice

blocks.title: Memory against nonlinearity
blocks.text: A reservoir with 20 linearly independent features has linear memory capacity 12. Can it also have total quadratic capacity 12?
solution: Total information-processing capacity over all orthogonal targets is at most the number of independent features, 20.

blocks.title: Shot budget
blocks.text: A 6-qubit reservoir behaves as fully scrambling. How many shots per step to resolve 20% of a Pauli feature's spread?

For a broad review start with Mujal and co-authors (2021); for the original proposal Fujii and Nakajima (2017); for universality Chen and Nurdin (2019) and Nokkala and co-authors (2021); for concentration Xiong and co-authors (2023); for measurement, Mujal and co-authors (2023).
